newsitem.title: CHINA: China private businessmen confident post-Deng.
newsitem.headline: China private businessmen confident post-Deng.

text.p: China's growing private business community on Thursday mourned the death of leader Deng Xiaoping, the man who made it possible to amass private wealth, but said they expected little change in economic policy after his death.
Deng, who died on Wednesday night, was the architect of China's economic reforms and the author of such slogans as "To get rich is glorious".
He allowed the revival of private business early in the 1980s over the opposition of many senior ideologues in the ruling Communist Party, but with the almost unanimous support of the Chinese people.

By the end of 1995, China boasted 654,000 private firms, mostly in the service sector, employing 8.22 million people with a total annual output value of more than 229.5 billion yuan ($27.6 billion), according to official figures.

An official with the Hope Group, one of the biggest private companies in China and a major producer of animal feed based in Sichuan province, said they had no concerns about a sudden change of policy undercutting their ambitious investment plans.
"The government's policy of continuing the reforms will not change despite the death of Deng Xiaoping, so we are confident about our company's future," the official said.
"I believe there will be little impact on the development of private firms," he said by telephone from Sichuan's Chengdu city.
The private sector in China's economy saw dramatic growth following a trip to south China by Deng in 1992.
That trip helped remove most of the fear among entrepreneurs of the political risks of going into business.
Deng said in his writings he believed the Communist Party's hold on power would be strengthened by economic prosperity and by putting more money into the pockets of every Chinese citizen.
"Deng is a great man. Without him, private business in China would not develop so quickly," said Cai Guangtian, who runs a highly profitable string of night schools in Shanghai.
"The main policy will not change (with his death), although there might be some impact on some small events and some regions," said Cai.

"We should appreciate Deng Xiaoping, because without him, we would not be as rich as we are today," said the boss of a construction materials trading company in the coastal city of Wenzhou, 350 km (217 miles) south of Shanghai.
"I am quite confident about the future of my business," he added. "Actually, we are soon going to expand by opening a trade company in the United States."
Wenzhou is renowned for having more private companies than any other city in China.
Private businesses in China are expected to account for 20.2 percent of the country's total gross national product (GNP) by the year 2000, the China Business Times said early this month.
